1	\section{Application: \texorpdfstring{$\Kstar$}{K*}-Aware Data Filtering}
2	\label{sec:filtering}
3	
4	We test whether $\Kempirical$ has predictive value for curation strategy selection, using a single-model setup (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) as proof of concept.
5	$\Kempirical = 2$ predicts that binary curation should suffice, and that graduated performance should converge toward binary as the decay steepness increases.
6	We compare six strategies on 30{,}000 documents (depths 0--5): (i)~\textbf{no-filter}, (ii)~\textbf{binary-ours} ($w = 1 - P(\text{synthetic})$ from 15D LightGBM), (iii)~\textbf{binary-Drayson}~\citep{drayson2025}, (iv)~\textbf{graduated} ($w = \exp(-\alpha \cdot \hat{d})$, $\alpha \in \{0.1,\ldots,0.9\}$), (v)~\textbf{surprisal} (retain above median), and (vi)~\textbf{DSIR}~\citep{xie2023dsir}.
7	We fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct via LoRA (rank~8, $\alpha_{\text{LoRA}}{=}16$) for 3 epochs on MMLU (a multitask language understanding benchmark) and HellaSwag (a commonsense reasoning benchmark) across 5 seeds (51 total runs: 5 base strategies $\times$ 5 seeds $+$ 5 graduated-$\alpha$ values $\times$ 5 seeds $+$ 1 base-model reference; this 100\% synthetic setting is an upper bound~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}).

11	\small

Binary-ours uses the 15D LightGBM depth classifier; Graduated applies exponentially decaying weights $w = \exp(-\alpha \hat{d})$. Mean $\pm$ std over 5 seeds. Full $\alpha$ sweep in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}.}
13	\label{tab:tab_filtering_main}

17	Binary-ours minimizes MMLU degradation most effectively (Table~\ref{tab:tab_filtering_main}), reducing the gap from $-$1.53\,pp (no-filter) to $-$0.77\,pp (${\sim}$50\% reduction; $p_{\text{corr}} < 0.05$ vs.\ all alternatives).
18	These effects are measured in a 100\% synthetic upper-bound setting; real-world contamination ratios are typically lower, and effect sizes would scale accordingly.
19	The strategy ordering is interpretable through $\Kempirical$: binary filtering exploits the one reliable boundary (0v1), while graduated strategies assign weights to depths 2--5 based on near-random classifier outputs, injecting noise.
20	Graduated filtering converges monotonically toward binary: at $\alpha{=}0.9$, it matches binary-ours on HellaSwag exactly ($\Delta = 0$, $p_{\text{corr}} = 1.00$) but remains significantly worse on MMLU ($p_{\text{corr}} = 0.011$).
21	DSIR is indistinguishable from no-filter, confirming that depth-aware features are necessary for curation in recursively contaminated corpora (Figure~\ref{fig:filtering_strategies} in Appendix).
22	Binary filtering retains a consistent advantage across contamination levels (10--50\%), with effect sizes diminishing 3--6$\times$ relative to the 100\% setting; graduated weighting remains indistinguishable from no-filter at all tested ratios, confirming that depth assignments beyond $\Kempirical$ inject noise regardless of severity (Appendix~\ref{sec:dose_response}).

\section*{Limitations}

Our findings are bounded by:
(1)~\emph{Scope}: model scale $\leq$14B (5 architecture families), English text (C4, Wikipedia, arXiv), four decoding strategies; arXiv $\Kempirical{=}3$ is confirmed with five models across four architecture families but with reduced sample size ($n{=}2{,}200$ per model).
(2)~\emph{Protocol}: prompt-chain (isolates text-intrinsic degradation); retrain-chain yields $\Kempirical{\geq}4$ (Pythia-1.4B LoRA; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}), reflecting additional model-adaptation artifacts beyond text-level information loss.
(3)~\emph{Threshold}: $\Kempirical$ ranges from 2--3 at $\theta{=}0.55$ to 1 at $\theta{=}0.70$; 8/9 configurations yield $\Kempirical{=}2$ at $\theta{=}0.60$ (Mistral-7B: $\Kempirical{=}1$).
(4)~\emph{Marginal boundary}: Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.002; cross-scorer validation drops this to $\Kempirical{=}1$ (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}). LLaMA-3.1-8B represents the most marginal $\Kempirical{=}2$ assignment, with the 1v2 CI lower bound within 0.3 percentage points of $\theta$.
(5)~\emph{Feature set}: the 15D features yield a feature-set-specific lower bound ($\Ktheory$ may be strictly higher); neural probe $\Kempirical$ is model-dependent ($3$ for Qwen, $2$ for Pythia/OLMo).
(6)~\emph{Segment length}: $\Kempirical{=}2$ confirmed for 128 and 256 tokens (CI lower $> \theta$); 512 tokens yields point estimate $\Kempirical{=}2$ but CI lower marginally below $\theta$ ($0.5979$), indicating the boundary weakens at longer generation lengths.
(7)~\emph{Curation applicability}: the filtering evaluation uses a single model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) and effect sizes diminish at lower contamination ratios (10--50\%); however, the strategy ordering (binary $>$ graduated $\approx$ no-filter) is consistent across all tested ratios (Appendix~\ref{sec:dose_response}).
Additional limitations (cross-model scoring sensitivity, feature ranking variability at the 1v2 boundary, structural composition confound analysis) appear in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}.

\begin{abstract}
Web-scale corpora are increasingly contaminated by recursive synthetic content, yet no method estimates a document's generational depth.
We measure the discrimination boundary $\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain distinguishable) using 15 statistical features and an OBD-LightGBM classifier.
Across 9 model configurations (5 architecture families, 1B--14B), 3 source domains, and 4 decoding strategies, $\Kempirical \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ at $\theta{=}0.60$ (Cohen's $h{\approx}0.20$): general web text yields $\Kempirical{=}2$ as the dominant mode (8/9 configurations), while structured academic text (arXiv) yields $\Kempirical{=}3$, validated across five models and four architecture families.
A single generation pass suffices to render general web text indistinguishable from deeper synthetic content, a \emph{one-wash laundering} effect.
Generator-independent statistical features, computed via a fixed reference scorer, enable 80--92\% cross-model transfer among continuation-mode generators with scorer-invariant feature ordering ($\rho > 0.90$), and cross-scorer validation is consistent with $\Kempirical$ being governed by the generation process rather than the scoring model.
Downstream, domain-appropriate $\Kempirical$ correctly predicts optimal curation granularity: when contamination causes detectable quality loss, binary filtering minimizes degradation most effectively for web text.

2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\begin{figure*}[t]
5	\centering
6	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/pipeline.pdf}
7	\caption{Generational depth estimation pipeline. Seed documents are recursively passed through a generation operator $G_\delta$ to produce a depth chain. Statistical features are fed to the OBD-LightGBM classifier for depth prediction.}
8	\label{fig:pipeline}
9	\end{figure*}
10	
11	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
12	\label{sec:formulation}
13	
14	A generation operator $G_\delta$ (LLM + decoding strategy $\delta$) produces successive generations $X \to Y_1 \to \cdots \to Y_K$, where $Y_k = G_\delta(Y_{k-1})$ and $Y_0 \triangleq X$ (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
15	This sequence forms a Markov chain.
16	By the Data Processing Inequality, $I(X; Y_1) \geq I(X; Y_2) \geq \cdots \geq 0$: the original signal degrades monotonically.
17	Together with Markov chain convergence, this guarantees a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations are indistinguishable.
18	
19	We define the operational lower bound:
20	\begin{equation}
21	  \Kempirical = \max\{k \geq 1 : \auc_{k-1,k} > \theta\},
22	  \label{eq:kstar}
23	\end{equation}
24	where $\auc_{k-1,k}$ is the point-estimate pairwise AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) and $\theta = 0.60$ is a small-effect-size threshold (Cohen's $h \approx 0.20$\footnote{$h = 2\arcsin\!\sqrt{0.60} - 2\arcsin\!\sqrt{0.50} \approx 0.2014$, a ``small'' effect size by Cohen's (1988) convention; we use this as a motivating analogy rather than a formal justification, since the permutation test and AUC gap (below) are the primary evidence.}; motivated below).
25	Bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals (CIs; 1{,}000 resamples) provide uncertainty quantification: we verify that boundary-pair CI lower bounds exceed $\theta$ and non-boundary-pair CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$ (Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
26	
27	\paragraph{Threshold choice.}
28	$\theta{=}0.60$ is supported by three independent lines of evidence.
29	First, it corresponds to Cohen's $h \approx 0.20$, a conventional small-effect-size boundary.
30	Second, a 10{,}000-iteration permutation test yields a 95th-percentile null of ${<}\,0.55$ and $p < 0.002$ for all boundary comparisons, placing $\theta{=}0.60$ well above the empirical null.
31	Third, and most critically, the conclusion $\Kempirical{=}2$ is insensitive to the exact threshold: 1v2 AUC values cluster at $0.61$--$0.70$ while 2v3 values cluster at $0.55$--$0.59$, creating a ${\sim}$5--11\,pp discontinuity that any $\theta \in [0.55, 0.65]$ would separate (Figure~\ref{fig:kstar_theta}; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
32	Only at extremes does $\Kempirical$ shift: $\theta{=}0.55$ yields $\Kempirical{=}3$ for two Qwen configurations; $\theta{=}0.70$ yields $\Kempirical{=}1$ across all configurations.
33	The downstream filtering evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:filtering}) uses the OBD classifier without re-optimizing $\theta$, avoiding circularity.
34	
35	\subsection{Features and Classifier}
36	\label{sec:features}
37	
38	Each document is characterized by a 15-dimensional feature vector spanning four groups: \emph{surprisal moments} (mean, std, skewness, kurtosis; 4~dims), \emph{surprisal derivatives} (mean and std of first- and second-order differences, plus first-order skewness; 5~dims), \emph{vocabulary diversity} (type-token ratio, hapax legomena ratio, self-BLEU; 3~dims), and \emph{frequency tail statistics} (frequency kurtosis, entropy, rare token fraction; 3~dims).
39	All features are computed from token-level surprisal values via an external scorer model (full definitions in Table~\ref{tab:s5_features}, Appendix).
40	Self-BLEU is computed within each CV fold using only same-fold, same-depth reference samples to prevent leakage; it ranks \#1 in 1/8 conditions (greedy decoding) but is absent from the top-3 in all 7 others.
41	Removing self-BLEU reduces mean $\auc_{1v2}$ by $< 1$\,pp across all models (14D $\Kempirical = 2$ for all 4 configurations; bootstrap CIs in Table~\ref{tab:selfbleu_ablation}); in deployment where depth labels are unavailable, self-BLEU can be replaced with corpus-level self-similarity or omitted with minimal performance loss.
42	Hand-crafted features enable cross-generator transfer without retraining and permit attribution of discriminative power to specific text properties.
43	
44	We use \emph{Ordinal Binary Decomposition} (OBD), decomposing the $(K{+}1)$-class problem into $K$ cumulative binary sub-classifiers, each estimating $P(\text{depth} > k \mid \mathbf{x})$ via LightGBM (hyperparameters in Table~\ref{tab:s6_lgbm_params}).
45	OBD achieves lower MAE than multiclass LightGBM (e.g., 0.984 vs.\ 1.016 on Qwen-rewrite) while maintaining superior pairwise $\auc$ (mean 0.6095 vs.\ 0.4883 for ordinal logistic regression).
46	
47	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
48	\label{sec:experimental_setup}
49	
50	We evaluate nine configurations spanning five architecture families (Table~\ref{tab:setup}): Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (rewrite and continuation modes), Qwen2.5-1.5B (base, continuation), Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B (all continuation except Qwen-rw).

52	Default decoding: nucleus $p{=}0.95$, $T{=}1.0$; decoding ablation covers greedy, $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$.
53	Continuation mode truncates seeds to 128 tokens and extends to 256; rewrite mode paraphrases the full text.
54	Evaluation: 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation grouped by seed document; pairwise $\auc$ as primary metric.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.

This gap cuts across multiple communities: binary detectors~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp} produce no depth estimate (Section~\ref{sec:binary_confidence}), membership inference~\cite{zawalski2026codec} addresses a different question, and the model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} provides no per-text tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} likewise ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone.

Knowing whether the discriminable depth is finite, and where it saturates, has direct practical consequences.
For data curation, the saturation point determines filtering granularity: if discrimination collapses at depth 2, graduated weighting beyond that boundary injects noise, and binary filtering becomes the principled choice.
Model collapse theory predicts monotonic quality degradation across generations, but existing analyses are population-level and provide no per-text measure of where degradation saturates.
$\Kempirical$ fills this gap by localizing the generation at which adjacent outputs become empirically indistinguishable.

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$.
We empirically measure $\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations) using 15 statistical features computed via a fixed reference scorer (Section~\ref{sec:features}) and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \geq 1$ where the pairwise $\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
  \item \textbf{First empirical measurement of $\Kempirical$} across 9 model configurations (5 architecture families, 1B--14B), 3 source domains, and 4 decoding strategies at $\theta{=}0.60$ ($p \leq 0.002$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
  Both supervised OBD and zero-shot frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) show no statistically significant difference beyond $\Kempirical$ (McNemar $p > 0.05$, $N{=}500$; Section~\ref{sec:why_kstar}).
  \item \textbf{Domain ordering invariance}: the hierarchy arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$) $>$ C4 ($\Kempirical{=}2$) $>$ Wikipedia ($\Kempirical{=}1$) is preserved across six models spanning four architecture families, three scales (1B--14B), and four decoding strategies, with domain structural complexity as the primary factor governing $\Kempirical$ (Section~\ref{sec:cross_domain}).
  \item \textbf{Generator-independent features}: 15 scorer-derived statistical features enable 80--92\% cross-model transfer among continuation-mode generators ($\rho > 0.90$ feature ranking preservation), making $\Kempirical$ measurement practical without generator-specific training (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a downstream validation, $\Kempirical{=}2$ correctly predicts the strategy ordering for web-text filtering: binary curation minimizes degradation most effectively (MMLU $0.5941$ vs.\ base $0.6018$; Section~\ref{sec:filtering}).

11	\subsection{Problem Formulation}
12	\label{sec:formulation}
13	
14	A generation operator $G_\delta$ (LLM + decoding strategy $\delta$) produces successive generations $X \to Y_1 \to \cdots \to Y_K$, where $Y_k = G_\delta(Y_{k-1})$ and $Y_0 \triangleq X$ (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
15	This sequence forms a Markov chain.
16	By the Data Processing Inequality, $I(X; Y_1) \geq I(X; Y_2) \geq \cdots \geq 0$: the original signal degrades monotonically.
17	Together with Markov chain convergence, this guarantees a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations are indistinguishable.
18	
19	We define the operational lower bound:
20	\begin{equation}
21	  \Kempirical = \max\{k \geq 1 : \auc_{k-1,k} > \theta\},
22	  \label{eq:kstar}
23	\end{equation}
24	where $\auc_{k-1,k}$ is the point-estimate pairwise AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) and $\theta = 0.60$ is a small-effect-size threshold (Cohen's $h \approx 0.20$\footnote{$h = 2\arcsin\!\sqrt{0.60} - 2\arcsin\!\sqrt{0.50} \approx 0.2014$, a ``small'' effect size by Cohen's (1988) convention; we use this as a motivating analogy rather than a formal justification, since the permutation test and AUC gap (below) are the primary evidence.}; motivated below).
25	Bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals (CIs; 1{,}000 resamples) provide uncertainty quantification: we verify that boundary-pair CI lower bounds exceed $\theta$ and non-boundary-pair CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$ (Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
26	
27	\paragraph{Threshold choice.}
28	$\theta{=}0.60$ is supported by three independent lines of evidence.
29	First, it corresponds to Cohen's $h \approx 0.20$, a conventional small-effect-size boundary.
30	Second, a 10{,}000-iteration permutation test yields a 95th-percentile null of ${<}\,0.55$ and $p < 0.002$ for all boundary comparisons, placing $\theta{=}0.60$ well above the empirical null.
31	Third, and most critically, the conclusion $\Kempirical{=}2$ is insensitive to the exact threshold: 1v2 AUC values cluster at $0.61$--$0.70$ while 2v3 values cluster at $0.55$--$0.59$, creating a ${\sim}$5--11\,pp discontinuity that any $\theta \in [0.55, 0.65]$ would separate (Figure~\ref{fig:kstar_theta}; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.

This gap cuts across multiple communities: binary detectors~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp} produce no depth estimate (Section~\ref{sec:binary_confidence}), membership inference~\cite{zawalski2026codec} addresses a different question, and the model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} provides no per-text tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} likewise ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone.

Knowing whether the discriminable depth is finite, and where it saturates, has direct practical consequences.
For data curation, the saturation point determines filtering granularity: if discrimination collapses at depth 2, graduated weighting beyond that boundary injects noise, and binary filtering becomes the principled choice.
Model collapse theory predicts monotonic quality degradation across generations, but existing analyses are population-level and provide no per-text measure of where degradation saturates.
$\Kempirical$ fills this gap by localizing the generation at which adjacent outputs become empirically indistinguishable.

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$.
We empirically measure $\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations) using 15 statistical features computed via a fixed reference scorer (Section~\ref{sec:features}) and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \geq 1$ where the pairwise $\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
  \item \textbf{First empirical measurement of $\Kempirical$} across 9 model configurations (5 architecture families, 1B--14B), 3 source domains, and 4 decoding strategies at $\theta{=}0.60$ ($p \leq 0.002$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
  Both supervised OBD and zero-shot frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) show no statistically significant difference beyond $\Kempirical$ (McNemar $p > 0.05$, $N{=}500$; Section~\ref{sec:why_kstar}).
  \item \textbf{Domain ordering invariance}: the hierarchy arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$) $>$ C4 ($\Kempirical{=}2$) $>$ Wikipedia ($\Kempirical{=}1$) is preserved across six models spanning four architecture families, three scales (1B--14B), and four decoding strategies, with domain structural complexity as the primary factor governing $\Kempirical$ (Section~\ref{sec:cross_domain}).
  \item \textbf{Generator-independent features}: 15 scorer-derived statistical features enable 80--92\% cross-model transfer among continuation-mode generators ($\rho > 0.90$ feature ranking preservation), making $\Kempirical$ measurement practical without generator-specific training (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a downstream validation, $\Kempirical{=}2$ correctly predicts the strategy ordering for web-text filtering: binary curation minimizes degradation most effectively (MMLU $0.5941$ vs.\ base $0.6018$; Section~\ref{sec:filtering}).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Estimates suggest that a substantial fraction of online text is machine-generated~\cite{sun2025aigt, spennemann2025quantifying}, and this share continues to rise.
When models train on the outputs of earlier models, the resulting multi-generational synthetic text degrades with each iteration: tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This degradation arises in both \emph{retrain-chains} (iteratively training on model outputs) and \emph{prompt-chains} (recursively generating from previous outputs without retraining); we study the latter, which isolates generation-level information loss from training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_limitations}).
Yet the dominant paradigm treats all machine-generated text identically, discarding the generational depth dimension.

This gap cuts across multiple communities: binary detectors~\cite{basani2026diveye, zhang2024minkpp} produce no depth estimate (Section~\ref{sec:binary_confidence}), membership inference~\cite{zawalski2026codec} addresses a different question, and the model collapse literature~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024selfconsuming, schaeffer2025position} provides no per-text tool.
Data selection methods~\cite{xie2023dsir, tirumala2023d4, drayson2025} likewise ignore recursive depth.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone.

Knowing whether the discriminable depth is finite, and where it saturates, has direct practical consequences.
For data curation, the saturation point determines filtering granularity: if discrimination collapses at depth 2, graduated weighting beyond that boundary injects noise, and binary filtering becomes the principled choice.
Model collapse theory predicts monotonic quality degradation across generations, but existing analyses are population-level and provide no per-text measure of where degradation saturates.
$\Kempirical$ fills this gap by localizing the generation at which adjacent outputs become empirically indistinguishable.

The Data Processing Inequality guarantees that information degrades monotonically across generations, motivating a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$.
We empirically measure $\Kempirical$ (the maximum depth at which a classifier reliably distinguishes adjacent generations) using 15 statistical features computed via a fixed reference scorer (Section~\ref{sec:features}) and an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest $k \geq 1$ where the pairwise $\auc_{k-1,k}$ exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep]
  \item \textbf{First empirical measurement of $\Kempirical$} across 9 model configurations (5 architecture families, 1B--14B), 3 source domains, and 4 decoding strategies at $\theta{=}0.60$ ($p \leq 0.002$; Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary}).
  Both supervised OBD and zero-shot frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) show no statistically significant difference beyond $\Kempirical$ (McNemar $p > 0.05$, $N{=}500$; Section~\ref{sec:why_kstar}).
  \item \textbf{Domain ordering invariance}: the hierarchy arXiv ($\Kempirical{=}3$) $>$ C4 ($\Kempirical{=}2$) $>$ Wikipedia ($\Kempirical{=}1$) is preserved across six models spanning four architecture families, three scales (1B--14B), and four decoding strategies, with domain structural complexity as the primary factor governing $\Kempirical$ (Section~\ref{sec:cross_domain}).
  \item \textbf{Generator-independent features}: 15 scorer-derived statistical features enable 80--92\% cross-model transfer among continuation-mode generators ($\rho > 0.90$ feature ranking preservation), making $\Kempirical$ measurement practical without generator-specific training (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}).
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a downstream validation, $\Kempirical{=}2$ correctly predicts the strategy ordering for web-text filtering: binary curation minimizes degradation most effectively (MMLU $0.5941$ vs.\ base $0.6018$; Section~\ref{sec:filtering}).
